in.other_title: In debate, judge (Guard) Elo rises with general intelligence while debater Elo stays flat
in.rationale: Kenton et al. define debate where a judge LLM answers after viewing two debater LLMs argue opposite answers, with 3 rounds by default. Engels et al.'s debate game is a 3-round debate modelled on Kenton et al., and they report judge (Guard) Elo rising with general intelligence while debater Elo stays flat on TruthfulQA, with similar behaviour on QuALITY and PrOntoQA.
in.scope: proposed DEPENDS_ON: debate scaling results that use a debate game modelled on Kenton et al.'s protocol

in.other_title: Lang et al. follow Kenton et al.'s assigned-role debate but feed transcripts to weak-model training
in.rationale: The passage states that the protocol follows Kenton et al. and changes what the debate is used for (training a weak supervisor instead of informing a weak LLM judge), which fits EXTENDS. Kenton et al. study inference-time judging with instruction-tuned models; Lang et al. use pretrained Qwen models.
in.scope: proposed EXTENDS: Assigned-role LLM debate used to help a weak model; holds where the weak model is trained on transcripts rather than acting as an inference-time judge

in.rationale: The authors explicitly agree with Kenton et al.'s remark that assigned-role consultancy is a weak baseline and use it to motivate replacing judge accuracy with ASD. This is agreement with an argument rather than with an empirical result.
in.scope: proposed SUPPORTS: Whether assigned-role (random) consultancy is an adequate baseline for judging debate's benefit.

in.rationale: The authors build on the LLM-judge setup of the cited oversight studies and name the change (persona conditioning), comparing against the conventional version in their own experiments. That is EXTENDS; it does not dispute Kenton et al.'s results, which come from different tasks.
in.scope: proposed EXTENDS: How LLM judges are configured in debate and consultancy experiments; the change is conditioning the judge on a persona with prior beliefs

text: The authors test consultancy, in which a judge LLM questions a single consultant LLM that argues for one of two options, and debate, in which the judge answers after viewing a debate between two debater LLMs arguing opposite answers. Each consultancy question is run with the consultant assigned the correct and, separately, the incorrect answer, which the authors say simulates a worst-case RLHF in which feedback cannot tell correct from incorrect answers; both are compared with direct QA baselines (QA with or without the article).
title: Assigned-role consultancy and debate with an LLM judge, compared with direct QA baselines
